name: page-controller
intent: Give each logical page or form its own input controller that handles the requests addressed to it — reading the request, invoking domain logic and choosing the view — instead of routing every request through one shared handler.
problem: Dynamic pages repeat the same request handling: parse and validate the incoming request, call domain logic, pick a view, report errors. Without a per-page home for that logic it either spreads into templates or gets copied into every script; the recurring decision is whether one page or form owns its request handling, or whether a central controller multiplexes all of them.
context: Server-side web presentation where URLs map one-to-one onto logical pages, forms or actions: CGI programs, servlets and JSP pages, controller actions, Razor Pages, route handlers in micro-frameworks. It fits sites whose pages share little behaviour, page-focused areas of larger applications, and frameworks whose native unit is a page; it stops fitting as soon as most pages need the same authentication, internationalisation, layout or tracing.
benefits: The structure mirrors the site: one URL, one handler, one page — trivial to navigate and to explain, with no dispatcher configuration beyond the mapping itself.
Page-specific request handling, model access and view selection sit together, so everything one page needs is in one place.
Pages evolve independently: adding or changing a page touches one handler, not a shared routing table or the other pages.
Each controller is separately invocable with a synthetic request/response, which makes page logic testable without the container.
No central bottleneck — work on different pages proceeds in parallel, and one page's failure is not routed through shared dispatch code.
Least machinery for small applications: the framework's per-page unit (servlet, page model, route function, route block) is used directly, without command objects or an extra dispatch layer.
Familiar and natural structure: each developer can own one or more pages end-to-end without understanding the whole system.
Explicit URL contract: the mapping from URL to handler is visible and deterministic, making routing easy to reason about.
tradeoffs: Behaviour common to many pages (authentication, authorisation, internationalisation, error pages, logging, layout) is duplicated in every controller unless it is factored into helpers or a base class — and a check forgotten on one page is a classic security failure mode.
A single cross-cutting change becomes an N-page edit, and the duplicated copies drift apart in wording and behaviour over time.
There is no central point at which request processing can be intercepted, reordered or decorated, so filters or middleware have to be bolted onto the container instead of into the controller.
Multi-step workflows are spread across pages: the flow exists only as links and redirects and cannot be read, tested or reused as a unit.
The URL contract is implicit in deployment or file layout (CGI path, servlet mapping, page location, annotation), so moving or renaming a controller can silently change or break public URLs.
As the site grows, shared abstractions creep into a base controller or superclass — a front controller in all but structure, with none of its explicitness.

Security checks are easy to omit on individual pages: each new page requires an explicit decision about whether it needs authentication and authorisation, and forgetting one is a vulnerability (cf. OWASP AC4 — Missing Function Level Access Control).
High fan-out for structural changes: renaming a shared layout or standard error page requires touching every controller.

participants.responsibility: Input controller for one logical page or action: parses and validates the request, invokes domain logic, decides the outcome and selects the view that renders it.
Template or renderer that turns the model data prepared by the controller into the response (one per page, or shared across pages).
Transaction script, domain model or service the controller delegates to; it knows nothing about HTTP and returns plain results or errors.
Container- or framework-provided request and response objects the controller consumes and produces; the boundary that keeps HTTP out of the domain logic.
Mechanism that selects the controller for an incoming URL: server/CGI path, servlet mapping or annotation, page file location, route table or route decorator.
Optional place where behaviour common to several page controllers is factored so it is not copied into each one; if it keeps growing it is a Front Controller waiting to be made explicit.

use_cases: Small to medium websites where each page has its own URL, its own data and its own template (CMS front ends, marketing pages with forms, internal tools).
Form-heavy areas where one page owns one interaction end to end: show the form, validate the submission, run one workflow, render the result.
Prototypes and scripting-era deployments where one program, servlet or route function per page is the natural deployment unit.
Page-focused corners of a larger application (account settings, an admin console) whose pages genuinely differ from one another.

Frameworks whose canonical unit is the page itself: Razor Pages (PageModel = Page Controller), ASP.NET Web Forms code-behind, Java Struts Actions, Django FBV (Function-Based Views) mapped one-per-URL, Flask route functions, PHP single-file-per-page.
Per-page Ajax callbacks that are tightly coupled to a specific page's data and logic, where extracting them into a shared controller would create artificial coupling.
Situations where page-specific code is large enough to warrant a dedicated class but small enough that a full command-object framework is overkill.

ASP.NET Core Razor Pages: each PageModel owns the handlers and view data for one page, with OnGet/OnPost methods providing a concrete page-controller unit for page-specific forms. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/razor-pages/?view=aspnetcore-10.0

Django function-based views: URLconf maps a URL pattern to one Python view function that receives HttpRequest and returns the page response, making small page-specific interactions explicit. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/6.1/topics/http/views/

Flask route functions: the route decorator binds a URL and HTTP methods to one view function, a lightweight Page Controller shape for independent pages and forms. https://flask.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/quickstart/
avoid_when: Many pages need the same authentication, internationalisation, layout or tracing: use Front Controller (plus Application Controller or Command objects for dispatch) so the behaviour exists once.
The pages are really one API surface with many actions: a Command dispatcher or Action-Domain-Responder is clearer than a page per endpoint.
The site is content without per-request logic: a Template View, a static file server or a CMS already suffices.
One process per page would multiply deployment and startup cost (classic CGI): consolidate behind a front controller or an application server.

The chosen framework already supplies routing plus middleware and per-action handlers (Rails, ASP.NET MVC, Express, Spring, Django): use that idiom instead of hand-building a page-controller hierarchy on top of it.
Complex multi-step workflows that span several pages: the flow cannot be read, tested or modified as a unit from any single page controller.
Highly consistent UI chrome, navigation or layout applied to every page: factor into a shared layout controller or template rather than duplicating in every handler.
pitfalls: Copying a previous page controller as a template, including its session checks and error handling — the duplicated authorisation then drifts page by page until one page silently omits a critical check (OWASP AC4).
Letting the controller grow into model and view: SQL, business rules and HTML in the handler make it untestable and unfixable in one place.
Assuming a shared check exists elsewhere: every new page needs its own explicit validation and authorisation, because nothing intercepts requests centrally.
Binding controller classes to view templates too tightly (e.g., returning HTML strings directly) so the view cannot be swapped without modifying the controller.
Omitting HTTP status codes: returning 200 for a missing resource (should be 404) or for validation failure (should be 400) misleads clients and breaks automated tooling.
Handling GET and POST in the same method without branching, causing CSRF vulnerabilities or duplicate submissions on back-button reload.

Making page controllers non-final in frameworks where inheritance causes route annotation conflicts (e.g., PHP Symfony/Zicht bundle where subclass routes silently override parent routes at the same path).

Letting the base controller grow into a hidden front controller: when shared methods exceed page-specific methods, the design has outgrown Page Controller and a formal Front Controller should be introduced.

Wrong move: use Page Controller as the application-wide policy boundary -> duplicated authentication, logging and error handling drift between URLs -> instead put shared policy in middleware, filters or a Front Controller and retain Page Controllers for page-specific work.
anti_patterns: Fat page controller: request handling, business rules, persistence and HTML generation all in one handler, so nothing can be tested or reused.
Copy-paste controller: every new page starts as a copy of the last, including its session checks and error handling, which then diverge quietly.
Hidden front controller: so much common behaviour is pulled into a base controller that every page runs the same code — a front controller with none of its structure or documentation.
Template scriptlets (JSP Model 1 style): domain logic written directly in the page template, so the page is controller, model and view at once and the logic is reachable only through the web server.

Per-resource monolithic controller (Anti-Pattern): one controller that owns all actions for one entity/resource regardless of page boundaries — conflates resource grouping with page grouping, leading to massive controllers that sacrifice the clarity of Page Controller's one-page-one-handler contract.
design_principles: Single responsibility: one controller owns the request handling of one page, and only that page.
Separation of concerns: the controller translates HTTP into domain calls and model data into a view; the domain stays HTTP-ignorant.
Open/closed in the small: a new page is a new handler, not a change to an existing dispatcher.
DRY applies to the shared surface: behaviour common to several pages is factored once (helper, filter, base class) — and if it keeps growing, the design has outgrown the pattern.
KISS / least machinery: choose the simplest structure that fits while pages genuinely differ, rather than pre-building a front controller for a site that does not need one.
Fail closed on security: every page controller must explicitly declare its access requirements; absence of an auth check is not a permission, it is a vulnerability (cf. OWASP AC4).
Explicit over implicit: URL routing should be declarative and visible in code or config, not inferred from file layout, to prevent silent public-URL changes during refactoring.
best_practices: Keep each controller thin: parse and validate the request, call domain logic, select a view or redirect — no business rules, no SQL, no markup generation.
Write shared checks (authentication, authorisation, validation, error handling) as helpers or container filters and invoke them from every page explicitly, so their absence is visible in a diff.
Map URLs explicitly (route table, annotation, explicit mapping) rather than relying on file layout alone, so refactoring never silently changes the public URL contract.
Use POST-redirect-GET for actions so a reload does not repeat the submission.
Give every page its own error path: a missing session or invalid input must produce a defined response, not a stack trace.
Watch the ratio: when most pages call the same shared helpers, migrate to a Front Controller (with Application Controller or Command objects) instead of enlarging a base controller.
Select views by convention: `UserProfileController` → `user_profile.html` reduces configuration boilerplate and makes the contract explicit.
Return the correct HTTP status codes: 200 for success, 400 for bad input, 401/403 for auth failures, 404 for missing resources, 500 for server errors.

Separate GET and POST handler concerns: use distinct methods or handler names (e.g., `OnGet`/`OnPost` in Razor Pages, `def get()`/`def post()` in Django FBV) to prevent CSRF and back-button duplicate submissions.
Make page controller classes `final` (or equivalent) in languages where subclass inheritance can cause routing conflicts, to prevent silent route override by subclasses.
Factor view-preparation logic into helpers or ViewModel objects so the controller remains a pure coordinator and the view remains a pure template.

Use a Layer Supertype (base Page Controller) for genuine shared behaviour (common data loading, layout lookup) but keep it thin; a supertype that exceeds its page-specific children in volume has become a hidden Front Controller.
Write page-level integration tests: simulate a request to each controller and verify the response status, headers and view selection — catching auth omissions and bad redirects early.

related_patterns_notes.front-controller: When shared cross-page behaviour (auth, i18n, logging) grows large enough to duplicate across many page controllers, the natural next step is to extract that behaviour into a single central handler — a Front Controller. Fowler: Page Controller 'works particularly well in a site where most of the controller logic is pretty simple' while 'Front Controller becomes compelling when you need to apply common behaviour to many pages consistently.' Many sites evolve from Page Controller toward Front Controller; Fowler notes it is 'not uncommon to have a mix in a site where some requests are dealt with by Page Controllers and others are dealt with by Front Controllers, particularly when a team is refactoring from one to another.
related_patterns_notes.application-controller: Often used together with Front Controller: Application Controller centralizes the dispatch decision (which action/view to run) while Page Controller handles the per-page request processing. When multiple pages share the same action selection logic (e.g., a workflow engine), Application Controller prevents that logic from being copied into each Page Controller.
related_patterns_notes.action-domain-responder: Paul M. Jones's ADR pattern clarifies the separation that Page Controller roughly sketches: Action = input collection + domain invocation (equivalent to the controller portion), Domain = business logic, Responder = HTTP response construction. ADR notes that the 'Controller' in 'Model 2' MVC mixes concerns; Page Controller as defined by Fowler shares this weakness. ADR is a more explicit separation of those same responsibilities.
related_patterns_notes.template-view: The View participant in Page Controller is often a Template View (JSP, Razor, PHP). Fowler notes that using a server page as both controller and view (the JSP-scriptlet style, sometimes called 'Model 1') works for simple display but becomes awkward when logic must choose between views or build request data. A separate Page Controller + Template View is the preferred pairing.
related_patterns_notes.transform-view: Alternative view strategy for Page Controller: instead of a template with embedded markup, a transform view converts domain data through a programmatic transform. Less common in modern frameworks but applicable when the same data must be rendered into multiple output formats.
related_patterns_notes.view-helper: Fowler recommends extracting complex request-parsing, data-formatting and view-preparation logic from the Page Controller into Helper objects (View Helpers). This keeps the controller thin while preventing logic from migrating into the template. Examples: JSP custom tags, Razor helper methods.
related_patterns_notes.composite-view: Page Controllers often delegate to a Composite View for the actual rendering: the controller prepares page-specific data and selects which sub-templates or portlets to compose, while the Composite View assembles the final page from those parts.
related_patterns_notes.page-cache: Whole-page caching at the HTTP or reverse-proxy layer works well with Page Controller: because each page has a clear controller-to-view mapping, the cached representation of a page is straightforward to invalidate or warm. The Page Controller can also decide at runtime whether to serve a cached response.
